questions.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{2}3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{3}3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{e}^{x}]}_{a}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{2}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =3\cdot ({e}^{2}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/115e3198226940a76b770f5942bb06e6496bd234d6cb5fee2d33f19038931bd3.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{2}3{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot ({e}^{2}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{a}) \\  & =3({e}^{2}-0) \\  & =3{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{x\cdot {5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{u}}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{5}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{x\cdot {5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{5}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{5}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{5}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{5}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{5}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/3cb8903ed53a713c5e23e4dbad4801788440954ac3a5f7e08ab1bd71cc9c631f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{x\cdot {5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.\end{aligned}
$$

| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{-\infty }{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{3u}}{3}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{3a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{3x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/34abda46dc9fc2c6f14ce4f8460ba076a16004bb9141eb8074cdc08e0c12fd2f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}}{\sqrt{3}}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{\sqrt{3}a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{\sqrt{3}x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/1c0fc31d392bbaccf9a292553321bd60ccbdb2a02f3675543797f570c4fa0ef1.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{\sqrt{3}a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving the Exponential Function
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\,]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-3x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^{-3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-3x} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-3x} =0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/bc4ffc41105491f2bd6b37b2482afc64946d8f67f6db83dfa322c400ae4bc2b6.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x} & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (0-{e}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving Other Exponential Functions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int b^{\,px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1{p\ln(b)} b^{\,px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{2}^{2x+1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {2}^{1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{2}^{2x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({2}^{0}-{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=2^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 2^{2x} = 0$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 2^{2x} = \infty$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/009f467677932d0ac17e1632c31f4d3aa5271ffe332730d9670e69862b243bef.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=x^4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 4x^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac 14 \textrm{d}u =x^3\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty$ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{2}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{2}^{-u}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{2^x},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = 0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/1969145d74662468ec23d458ac1ad0194d51cbf6b026718b7232466e9357efdf.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$
